title: Just a teacher, standing in front of a teacher, asking them not to perform
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Writing as a trust-level observer herself, Haili Hughes argues that lesson observation too often prompts teachers to perform 'watchability' rather than teach as they normally would, and that this reflects a wider culture in which wisdom is assumed to grow with distance from the classroom. She concedes that consultants and trust staff can offer real value but warns against confusing perspective with authority, or distance with clarity. Teaching is difficult, she argues, because it depends on minute-by-minute judgement under uncertainty, and most of that work is invisible to an outsider. Observation offers only a sliver of practice, yet observers turn thin evidence into thick conclusions and reward the performance cues that are most legible to them. What schools need instead is honest professional dialogue in which teachers can admit failure and examine their decisions, requiring humility, vulnerability and mutual respect from observers and mentors. She closes by calling for professional esteem to be redirected toward classroom teachers, insisting the classroom is the core business rather than something one graduates from.
points: Hughes argues observation distorts the thing it measures: teachers perform 'watchability' for the lanyarded visitor rather than teaching as they usually do.
She names a cultural drift in which wisdom is assumed to rise with distance from the classroom, so that consultants' preferences harden into principles and their anecdotes into frameworks.
Observers turn thin evidence into thick conclusions, rewarding legible performance cues while missing invisible judgement such as a deliberate decision not to intervene.
Improvement depends on honest professional dialogue about decisions, which demands humility and vulnerability from the observer as well as the teacher.
quotes: It is a problem because teaching is already difficult enough without layering performance anxiety on top of it. It is a problem because classrooms are full of human beings, not lab conditions.

Somewhere along the way, we have started behaving as though wisdom in education increases in direct proportion to distance from the classroom. The further away someone is from Year 9 on a wet Thursday afternoon, the more seriously they are sometimes taken.
But the problem begins when we confuse perspective with authority, or distance with clarity. The view from above is not always the truest one. Sometimes it is simply the least interrupted.
Teaching is not difficult because nobody has yet discovered the correct five-step method and hidden it in a slide deck. It is difficult because it depends on judgement.
Too often, though, we do the opposite. We turn thin evidence into thick conclusions. We watch twenty minutes and talk as if we have seen the teacher.
That kind of dialogue is harder than handing down tips. It is slower, messier and less flattering to the person leading it.
It would do the profession good to say this more plainly: the classroom is not the conference league. It is not the place you graduate from into proper educational influence. It is the core business.
